Christa Pike describes constant pain in first statement since her failed execution
articles.description: Christa Pike describes constant pain in first statement since her failed execution AP News ‘My Body Hurts’: Pike Describes Pain and Isolation After Botched Execution The New York Times US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution BBC Doctor Who Oversaw Christa Pike’s Botched Execution Still Wants Her Put to Death People.com Christa Pike, in first statement since botched execut
articles.content: Christa Pike said Friday she remains in constant pain, struggles to speak and has been largely isolated in a prison hospital after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month. In her first public statement since, Pike said she’s “deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.” “I continue to think about my victim’s family,” she said, “and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.” Pike and her boyfriend tortured and stabbed a 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, to death in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time, making her one of the youngest women sentenced to death. Slemmer’s mother traveled from Florida to witness Pike’s execution. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably didn’t enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered. Unconscious, she was hospitalized on a ventilator for days, and at one point her lawyers said they didn’t expect her to survive. “There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” Pike said. “And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.” Pike said she had been prepared to die in peace, but instead woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed. She said she’s “searching for meaning in what happened to me.” “I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” Pike said in a statement dictated to her legal team from prison. Pike remains sentenced to die, and her attorneys want Republican Gov. Bill Lee to change that to life in prison. However, Lee told reporters this week, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.” The governor has tapped a former U.S. attorney to conduct an independent review of the failed execution, and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled for this year. Pike’s attorneys, meanwhile, asked a federal judge Friday to allow her to interact with other prisoners instead of being isolated in the infirmary. They said her isolation violates a 2024 agreement that ended her mostly solitary confinement and allowed her to work, eat, exercise and have social contact with other women. “Her renewed isolation has caused, and will continue to cause, significant psychological harm and trauma,” Pike’s legal team wrote. Pike’s lethal injection was plagued by problems. Her attorneys had warned that her small veins and diagnosis of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting disorder, could make IV access difficult. In a court document, her attorney Randy Spivey said the execution team struggled to get working IV lines in Pike’s arms and expressed concern that a vein might be “blowing.” Pike remained awake for much of the lethal injection, saying her arm hurt and burned before falling unconscious. The execution began just before 7:30 p.m. and an ambulance arrived at the prison about an hour and 45 minutes later. The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. In a 2025 deposition released with court documents this week, prison Warden Kenneth Nelson said the execution team doesn’t practice inserting IV lines during training sessions, at the directive of the prison commissioner. Nelson said he did not know why the practice was discontinued or when the order was given. Practicing insertion of IVs was part of Tennessee’s prior execution protocol, but it is not included in the state’s new protocol. Dorinda Carter, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction, said she could not comment on the filing because of pending litigation. Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike’s failed execution. The governor named Christopher Hansen as interim commissioner.

articles.title: Michigan elections: School districts seeking nearly $4 billion in bonds
articles.description: School districts are asking voters to borrow money for infrastructure projects. Leaders say they know families are facing increased household costs, but their options are limited.
articles.content: While the race for governor and US Senate continues to dominate the airwaves in Michigan, flying under the radar are more than 100 ballot questions to raise money for schools. Forty-two districts are asking voters to approve school bonds on Tuesday’s ballot, according to Gongwer News Service. Find out what's on your ballot, learn about the candidates and issues, check the facts and get the information you need to make informed decisions. From voter guides to election resources, we've got you covered. In total, districts are asking for nearly $4 billion in bonds for everything from constructing new buildings to fixing bathrooms and buying buses. The requests come as voters face rising prices and as it’s increasingly challenging to get bonds approved.Many of the districts requesting bonds are trying again after a previous proposal failed. “If a district needs to raise (money) for repairs, upgrades, new buildings, whatever that may be, the only way they can do that is via these types of bond campaigns,” said Robert McCann, executive director of the K-12 Alliance of Michigan, a group of 123 school districts. Districts spend the majority of their operating funds on employee wages and benefits. That leaves little left for building upgrades, renovations or purchases. Many districts face aging infrastructure and have sought state funds to pay for updating facilities.One estimate finds that public school districts need nearly $23 billion in repairs, more than the entire state K-12 budget this fiscal year.In July, the state awarded $224 million in grants to 31 school districts for school repairs. Another $100 million in grants is available but “much more is needed,” said Michigan Department of Education spokesperson Bob Wheaton. “The Michigan Department of Education has advocated for and will continue to advocate with our partners in the Legislature for more infrastructure funding so that students and educators have the school facilities they need for students to learn.” McCann said bonds are “Band-Aids to the larger problem” of school infrastructure funding. “There has to be a broad look at how we solve this problem with a dedicated funding stream for state support for school infrastructure,” he said. Dearborn Public Schools, the third largest district in the state, has the largest school bond on the ballot. The district is seeking approval for a $1.5 billion bond “to build new schools, improve safety across the district, add hands-on STEAM learning spaces, renovate at every school, and eventually ensure that every school is air-conditioned.” “It’s going to be revolutionary, and it’s what our students deserve, no doubt about it,” said Superintendent Mike Esseily. Some boiler systems are 50-60 years old, and the average of a building in the district is 71 years old, said Esseily. Eastpointe Community Schools is asking voters to approve a $99 million bond for projects such as updated classrooms and restrooms and new HVAC systems. The district’s nearly century-old high school building does not have air conditioning in classrooms.The district also plans to merge the middle school and high school into one building and upgrade to the district’s early learning center. Superintendent Christina Gibson said consolidating would allow for more college and career programming and cut down on operating costs like cleaning and utilities. Gibson said she feels for families with rising costs and has tried everything she can to avoid making this request. In February she tried to secure a $25 million state budget earmark. She also sought a state grant specifically for infrastructure. “We’re trying to provide high quality educational experiences for our children,” Gibson said. If the Dearborn bond passes, the district would stop collecting its operating millage. Esseily said leaders are “very cognizant” that residents are experiencing higher costs and sees the decision to not collect the operating millage as a “kind of our way to really meet residents hopefully where they’re at, and make it appealing to them.” Jason Helsen, associate executive director of Michigan School Business Officials, said voters are asking “healthy questions” about bonds and the state’s foray into infrastructure grants shows the state is grappling with the “big dollar question” of funding school infrastructure. School districts have three types of funding proposals on the ballot: bond issues; sinking funds, which are a kind of pay-as-you-go account funded by property taxes, and operating millages. Communities are also asking voters to approve taxes for libraries, roads and public safety. Seven communities have marijuana proposals on the ballot. Michigan schools use a combination of local, state and federal funds. Some communities are trying again to raise funds after previous efforts have failed. Gwinn Area Community Schools is trying for a $24.95 million bond. It’s the fifth time in recent years the district has tried to pass a bond. Comstock Public Schools is requesting a $23.7 million bond Tuesday after bond efforts failed in May 2026 and November 2025. Brighton Area Schools, Hopkins Public Schools, Meridian Public Schools and Yale Public Schools are all pitching bonds that are smaller than rejected proposals from May. FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
articles.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP).
articles.content: Groundbreaking therapy provides additional treatment option that fights the disease at its source, not only its symptoms The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options. “Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER). “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.” The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit. RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11). Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells. The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment. The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site. The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Media:FDA Request for Comment202-690-6343 The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

articles.title: Suspect in killings of Oberlin professor, wife held on $3 million bond
articles.description: Suspect in killings of Oberlin professor, wife held on $3 million bond AP News Oberlin College Professor and His Wife Are Murdered by His Son, Police Say The New York Times Beloved Oberlin professor and his wife killed by his son, police say The Columbus Dispatch Oberlin College professor and wife found fatally shot at home; son charged with murder NBC News In Memory of Pipo Nguyen-duy and Trần Nam Phong The Oberlin
articles.content: COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — An Oberlin College professor and his wife are dead, and the educator’s 31-year-old child is being held on a $3 million bond and facing murder charges in their deaths. The bodies of Pipo Nguyen-Duy, 64, a studio art and photography professor and acclaimed fine art photographer, and his wife, Tran Thi Nam Phong, 56, were found shot in their home a few blocks off campus on Wednesday, according to police. The professor was on the first floor of the home, his wife on the second. Asia Nguyen-Duy, previously known as Daniel Jones, of Ashland, Oregon, was arraigned Thursday on charges of murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence, according to court filings. A motive has not yet been released. The younger Nguyen-Duy, face tattooed and bloodied, was initially carried into the municipal courtroom before later being wheeled in seated on a chair. The suspect said they are gender neutral and no longer go by the name Daniel Jones. Identification found in a car that police found set afire near the college’s conservatory of music, which led them to the scene of the crime, listed the name Daniel Jones. Oberlin City Prosecutor Zachary Simonoff told the judge that the accused had offered a confession to the crimes and led them to the father and stepmother’s address. Simonoff also told Oberlin Municipal Court Judge Farah Emeka that the defendant’s mother had been in touch with police to let them know that her child was “currently psychotic” and needed medication. A message was left with Asia’s attorney. The case has been bound over to Lorain County Common Pleas Court, where it will next go before a grand jury. The suspect is being held in the Lorain County Jail. The deaths have rocked the private liberal arts college, where students had just returned this week from fall break. Studio art classes were paused or modified in the wake of the professor’s death. An exhibit of his internationally acclaimed photography was placed on display at the campus art museum to provide students, alumni and collaborators a place to gather and reflect. A memorial tribute for Nguyen-Duy, who arrived at Oberlin in 1998, also is being planned. Digital forums for sharing condolences and memories also were set up by Oberlin and some regional institutions, including the Museum of Contemporary Art Cleveland. Carmen Twillie Ambar, president of Oberlin College and Conservatory, called it “a deeply challenging moment for our community.” “Tragedies such as this one intrude upon our lives in jarring ways,” she wrote in an open letter. “I am simply overwhelmed with sadness, and I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community.” Pipo Nguyen-Duy was also mourned by the Guggenheim Foundation, where he was a 2011 photography fellow. The foundation said he immigrated to the U.S. from Vietnam in 1975 and took up photography in his late 20s. He had a bachelor’s degree in economics from Carleton College and both a master of arts and a master of fine arts degree from the University of New Mexico at Albuquerque. “In his wide-ranging body of work, Nguyen-duy considered immigration and emigration, intimacy, abandonment and decay, cultural assimilation, and the cost of war,” the foundation said on Instagram.

articles.title: AI law firm Crosby bids on disintegrating, famed firm Weil Gotshal
articles.description: Like a real-life episode of "Suits," the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry. And now an AI firm has entered the picture.
articles.content: Like a real-life episode of “Suits,” the demise of famed white-shoe Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has been the talk of the legal industry this week. And now Silicon Valley has entered the picture. Two-year-old AI-first law firm Crosby has put in a bid to buy some of the assets of Weil Gotshal, including its trademark, its brand, and some unspecified internal data, TechCrunch has confirmed. Separately, it is also working to hire some of the firm’s 1,200 lawyers. The Information was first to report this offer. The once-prestigious Weil Gotshal confirmed to the New York Times this week that it was preparing to vote on dissolution in the coming days. The wind-down is happening after the firm’s presumed leadership heir apparent turned down the role, a number of its top-producing lawyers left, and a hoped-for merger with its rival, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, was shelved, the Times reported. Meanwhile, Crosby’s founders believe they are the future of law firms. Rather than selling their internally developed AI tech to existing firms like Harvey or Legora, Crosby is an actual law firm. It uses its AI to provide legal services at, the startup promises, a speed never before possible. The startup has raised about $85 million, including a $60 million Series B round in March led by Lux and Index, with participation from its seed-lead Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors, and Bain Capital Ventures. Crosby came out of stealth mode in 2025 armed with $5.8 million in seed money. Terms of the bid weren’t disclosed and there’s no guarantee that Crosby will prevail. But if it does, Weil Gotshal’s legacy could somehow rise from the ashes, transformed by an AI-first firm. articles.title: DOJ again warns election officials of potential criminal prosecution, days before midterm elections
articles.description: The letters, sent to all 50 states, remind officials to preserve election records. They come one day after a federal judge warned the Trump administration to stop threatening election workers.
articles.content: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for our free weekly newsletter to get the latest. The Justice Department has sent yet another round of letters to state election officials warning them that they could face criminal prosecution for violating federal election laws, this time reminding them that they must preserve ballots, voter-registration records, and other election materials for 22 months after a federal election. Multiple state election offices confirmed to Votebeat that they received identical letters dated Oct. 29 and signed by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. Officials familiar with the correspondence said the letters appear to have been sent to all 50 states. “It is a crime to willfully fail to comply with Section 20701,” the letter said, according to a copy provided to Votebeat. Votebeat also viewed letters sent to other states, which were identical. “Such a failure is punishable by up to a year in prison and a $1,000 fine.” The letter also warns that it is unlawful to willfully steal, destroy, conceal, mutilate, or alter election records. The letters, dated Thursday, Oct. 29, came two days after a federal judge in California verbally admonished the Trump administration for threatening election officials with criminal prosecution in a separate dispute over ballots cast by suspected noncitizens. “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately,” U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said during Tuesday’s hearing. In a written ruling Wednesday, Carter rejected the DOJ’s attempt to force California to set aside ballots from roughly 20,000 voters and reiterated his warning: “These threats must stop.” Justin Levitt, a former Justice Department official and White House voting rights adviser under President Joe Biden, said he was unaware of any precedent for sending such a reminder to election officials nationwide. “Election officials know that they have an obligation to comply with this law — they know that real, real well — and this certainly looks like it’s meant to intimidate rather than to inform,” Levitt said. Votebeat asked the Justice Department why the letters were sent just days before Election Day, why McCotter personally signed them, and whether similar reminders had been issued before previous federal elections. The department had not responded as of publication. The letters are the latest in a series of warnings from the Trump administration to state election officials. A July mailing warned officials they could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote, while September letters threatened civil or criminal penalties for failing to preserve records from the 2024 election. The July letters were signed by Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general overseeing the Justice Department’s civil rights division. The September letters, signed by Eric Neff, the acting chief of the division’s voting section, directed 29 states and Washington, D.C., to preserve records in connection with ongoing litigation over access to voter-registration data. Dhillon described those notices at the time as standard litigation practice rather than threats. The October letters, by contrast, cite an existing preservation requirement dating to 1960 without identifying a particular violation or pending investigation. They were also signed by a more senior official: McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general and the department’s second-highest-ranking official, who assumed the role in August. McCotter has recently played a direct role in the Justice Department’s election-related litigation. Earlier this month, he signed letters to California officials, including Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, demanding that they investigate a federal list of suspected noncitizens who had received mail ballots. He gave officials 48 hours to review the list and instructed them to set aside ballots from voters whose citizenship could not be confirmed, warning that the Justice Department would seek emergency court intervention. The Justice Department subsequently sued California, asking a judge to bar the state from counting the ballots of voters on the list. State and county officials disputed the accuracy of the federal government’s data, saying it included U.S. citizens and people who were not registered to vote. Carter rejected the department’s request Wednesday, finding that the proposed intervention could disrupt voting and prevent eligible citizens from having their ballots counted. The Justice Department appealed, and has since issued grand jury subpoenas to California election officials. Levitt said there was nothing inherently improper about the Justice Department reminding officials of their legal obligations, but such reminders are typically prompted by concerns about compliance or understanding of the law. “It is not itself improper,” Levitt said. “But it’s super weird that the deputy sent this letter, and it’s super weird he sent the letter to everybody.” Joshua Douglas, an election law professor at the University of Kentucky, also questioned the timing, particularly when election officials are occupied with preparations for Election Day. “I have never seen the DOJ send this kind of letter across the country in the days before the election,” Douglas said. The letters impose no new legal requirements, Douglas said, but create another issue for election officials to deal with during an already demanding period. “At least they aren’t targeting based on politics, but it feels very unnecessary and creates confusion,” he said. The nationwide mailing also comes as federal courts scrutinize other Justice Department demands to states. On Thursday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the department by noon today to disclose which states had received letters demanding that ballots from suspected noncitizens be set aside. Votebeat reporters Natalia Contreras, Carter Walker, Alexander Shur, Dion Nissenbaum, Hayley Harding, and Sasha Hupka contributed. Jessica Huseman is Votebeat’s editorial director and is based in Dallas. Contact Jessica at jhuseman@votebeat.org. Zohran Mamdani Says $17 Billion Instacart Takeover Means ‘Higher Prices and Harsher Exploitation,’ DoorDash CEO Says It’ll Make Delivery Cheaper
articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday that DoorDash Inc.'s (NASDAQ:DASH) $17 billion deal to buy Instacart will raise prices for the city, but the company's CEO Tony Xu said it will make delivery faster and more affordable. On Thursday, DoorDash agreed to acquire Maplebear Inc. (NASDAQ:CART), which does business as Instacart, for $65 per share, a 26% premium to its Oct. 22 close. "Corporate consolidation means higher prices, harsher exploitation, and greater economic inequality for New Yorkers," Mamdani said in a post on X. He added that the company "couldn't seem to find the money" to pay delivery workers until his administration forced it to give back more than $131 million in wages and penalties. Just last month, DoorDash couldn't seem to find the money to pay their deliveristas — until our administration forced them to give back $131M+ in stolen wages and penalties.This week, they've managed to find $17 billion to acquire one of their main competitors.Corporate… https://t.co/EUnynAhrSx — Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@NYCMayor) October 29, 2026 DoorDash and Instacart did not immediately respond to Benzinga's request for comment on the Mayor's post. Xu said on the company's third-quarter earnings call on Thursday that Instacart's orders unique to its network would add density to the last-mile network, bringing "efficiencies to offer faster delivery as well as lower cost throughout the system." He said that would "enable more affordable prices," generating more sales for grocers and retailers and more earnings opportunity for shoppers. Last month, DoorDash agreed to a $131.5 million settlement with the city over late and missing worker payments, admitting it "screwed up" while maintaining that its on-call pay method was legal. "We've stood up to these giants before. That doesn't stop now," Mamdani said. Earlier this year, Mamdani backed the Delivery Protection Act, a City Council bill meant to hold Amazon.com, Inc. accountable for what he called an exploitative business model that uses subcontractors to avoid responsibility for delivery workers. articles.title: El-Sayed and Stevens to make rare joint appearance as Democrats seek unity in Michigan Senate race
articles.content: DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign Sunday in Detroit alongside former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens, marking their first public appearance together in months after a week in which lingering divisions spilled into public view. The two will be joined by South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the country’s most prominent Black politicians, at a get-out-the-vote event at a Detroit church, according to two people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to discuss them publicly. The event was first reported by The Associated Press. The joint appearance — their first since a Democratic unity breakfast days after the Aug. 4 primary — follows weeks of Democrats struggling to unite behind El-Sayed following his razor-thin victory over Stevens. She received significant support from the Jewish and Black communities, leading to concerns about turnout in the general election. Tensions again spilled into public view Wednesday when Stevens’ fiancé, Jason Turkish, told The Detroit News that he would vote for Republican Mike Rogers. Hours later, Stevens appeared on CNN to reaffirm that she would be voting for El-Sayed, but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.” She said El-Sayed needs to reach out to people who were part of her coalition and “make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.” Asked Thursday evening about the upcoming event with Stevens, El-Sayed said “we’re always trying to unify the party” and it hadn’t happened sooner because of their busy schedules. El-Sayed then criticized the reporter for the question, saying “nobody cares” about internal party dynamics when the cost of living is so high. El-Sayed and Stevens last appeared together on Aug. 6, two days after the primary. Stevens pledged to support El-Sayed, telling CBS News she would do “whatever he wants me to do” on the campaign trail. But divisions from the contentious primary have persisted. Nearly $60 million was spent on advertising attacking El-Sayed, including $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel who represents a district with a large Jewish community in Detroit’s suburbs. The church visit on Sunday is intended to further that elusive unity, although its impact is uncertain, given that it comes just two days before the election. Michigan early voting started Oct. 24. “We’ve got a Black and Jewish coalition that came out and voted for me in droves. And I want them to come out and vote for Democrats,” Stevens said to CNN on Wednesday. El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel, past remarks and his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker have long drawn concern from some in Michigan’s large Jewish community. Turkish and others have said El-Sayed hasn’t done enough to address concerns ahead of the general election. The latest controversy centered on an ad by Rebellion PAC, an independent left-wing group, that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. “That has nothing to do with our campaign,” El-Sayed said of the ad. “It’s certainly not what I want to be talking about right now.” Stevens and other Democrats urged him to go further to denounce the content of the advertisement rather than merely distancing himself from it. Republicans face political challenges of their own, particularly voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the Iran war and high costs. Rogers has remained closely aligned with the president on most issues, appearing alongside him at a Michigan rally Sunday where he credited Trump with bringing manufacturing jobs back to the state. The rally took place in Port Huron, just across the river from Canada, a country with deep economic ties to Michigan that Trump has targeted with tariffs. El-Sayed has held campaign events in heavily Republican areas, including Michigan’s Upper Peninsula. His team also released an ad featuring clips of prominent conservative figures praising him, including former Fox News host Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism that he denies. But the ad created another source of friction with some Jewish voters. Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield criticized both the Rebellion PAC ad and El-Sayed’s campaign ad during a call with reporters. “We are one week away from the election, and it feels like the temperature has turned way up,” Starr said. “Instead of things getting better over the last seven weeks, they’ve actually gotten worse.” Rogers, meanwhile, appeared Wednesday with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas at an event hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition in Birmingham, Michigan. Cruz called antisemitism “a poison that is ripping the country apart” and accused Democrats of being taken over by “self-proclaimed communists and Islamists.” Trump has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, calling him a “jihadist” and saying Sunday that he was “on the side of terrorists.” Both candidates are trying to win over Black voters, particularly in Detroit’s Wayne County, where Stevens defeated El-Sayed in the Democratic primary. El-Sayed’s event with Stevens and Clyburn is part of an effort to shore up support among Black voters. Much of El-Sayed’s final campaign stretch has included appearances in Detroit. Rogers has also sought to make inroads with Black voters. He visited a reading remediation program at a Detroit high school and discussed housing costs with residents in Pontiac, north of the city. Earlier this month, his wife handed out $10 gift cards at a gas station. The gesture drew criticism from Ruby Farmer, a 68-year-old Detroit retiree. “You’re giving out gas cards in the inner city; you never would come for any other reason,” Farmer said. While Farmer has a bit of difficulty pronouncing El-Sayed’s name, she cast her ballot for him three weeks ago anyway. El-Sayed has come out in opposition to policies by Trump — policies Farmer says directly impact her family. “I have a special-needs son,” said Farmer. “He depends on Medicaid. Medicaid has been cut, and for home care workers in Michigan, all the benefits are on hold.” Cappelletti reported from Washington. Mike Householder contributed from Kalamazoo, Michigan.
